relationship: Narrative retrospective reference: the woman whose son Elisha revived
rationale: The famine instruction identifies its recipient by the son Elisha revived; the earlier account narrates the dead child, Elisha’s prayer, the opened eyes and the son returned to the Shunammite woman, grounding that particular identification.

relationship: Same-chapter instruction and compliance: the seven-year sojourn
rationale: The woman and household sojourn in the foreigners’ land for seven years according to Elisha’s word; the instruction had expressly named her household, sojourning and the seven-year famine, without prescribing that particular foreign destination.

relationship: Same-chapter appeal and royal response: recovering house and fields
rationale: After seven years the woman asks the king about her house and fields; the king subsequently orders restoration of her belongings and field produce from her departure onward, preserving the order without separately claiming its execution is narrated.

relationship: Same-chapter request and reported answer: Gehazi recounts the revived son
rationale: The king asks Gehazi to recount Elisha’s great works; the next notice names the revival of a dead son as the story being told when the woman appears, without claiming it is an exhaustive list of those works.

relationship: Narrative retelling: the revived child identified before the king
rationale: Gehazi identifies the woman and son while recounting Elisha’s revival of a dead son; the earlier account supplies the dead child, prayer, opened eyes and return to the mother, rather than a different revival narrative.

relationship: Narrative contrast: an earlier royal-help question and the later restoration order
rationale: Elisha earlier asks whether the woman has a matter for the king or commander, and she answers that she lives among her own people; here the king orders restoration after her own appeal, linking the different stated situations.

relationship: Same-chapter narrative continuity: the ill Syrian king sends to the newly arrived prophet
rationale: The son of Ader is ill when Elisha reaches Damascus and is reported there; Hazael then approaches Elisha with that king’s recovery inquiry, identifying the particular illness behind the visit.

relationship: Narrative contrast: two ill kings seek an oracle from different sources
rationale: The Syrian king directs an inquiry of the Lord through the man of God; Ahaziah had directed an inquiry of Baal Fly and received Elijah’s challenge about God in Israel. Their messengers, recipients and resulting words are kept distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter instruction and reported execution: Hazael’s recovery inquiry
rationale: Hazael brings the king’s recovery question to Elisha after being directed to inquire through the man of God; his reported load of Damascus goods and forty camels remains additional to the original manaa instruction.

relationship: Same-chapter oracle report and subsequent death: both clauses remain visible
rationale: Elisha gives the You will surely live message and says the Lord has shown certain death; Hazael reports the live clause, while the next-day account reports death and Hazael becoming king. The two oracle clauses are not silently harmonized.

relationship: Same-chapter emotional response and explanation: the man of God weeps
rationale: The verse ends with the man of God weeping; Hazael asks why, and Elisha names the evils he knows Hazael will do to Israel. The link does not assign the earlier ambiguous standing-and-held-face pronouns independently.

relationship: Prophetic warning and later oppression: Hazael afflicts Israel
rationale: Elisha foresees Hazael’s violence against Israel; the later reign account says Israel is given into Hazael’s hand and describes Syrian affliction. It supports the named oppression without separately verifying every foretold atrocity in that later passage.

relationship: Prophetic succession connection: Hazael named for Syria’s kingship
rationale: Elisha tells Hazael that the Lord has shown him reigning over Syria; the earlier word to Elijah directs the anointing of Hazael as Syria’s king. This links the named kingship without claiming an anointing ceremony is narrated here.

relationship: Same-chapter selective report: the live clause repeated and the death clause omitted
rationale: Hazael reports Elisha saying You will surely live; Elisha’s recorded words also include the Lord showing certain death. The connection marks the specific reported clause without treating it as the complete oracle.

relationship: Same-chapter prediction and royal succession: Hazael becomes king
rationale: The next-day account reports the machma dipped in water, the death and Hazael becoming king in his place; Elisha had expressly announced seeing Hazael reigning over Syria. The object and face pronouns are preserved rather than independently translated or reassigned.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Joram succeeds Jehoshaphat in Judah
rationale: Kings distinguishes Joram son of Ahab in Israel from the newly reigning Joram son of Jehoshaphat in Judah; Chronicles names Jehoshaphat’s death and his son Joram’s succession, without supplying Kings’ fifth-year synchronism.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Joram’s accession age and reign length
rationale: Both give Joram an accession age of thirty-two and eight years reigning in Jerusalem, matching the stated figures and city rather than importing an additional chronology.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Ahab’s daughter and Joram’s conduct
rationale: Both connect Joram’s marriage to Ahab’s daughter with walking in the way of Israel’s kings and Ahab’s house and doing evil before the Lord; neither passage is changed into an additional maternal genealogy.

relationship: Covenantal narrative parallel: David and the continuing lamp
rationale: Kings says the Lord would not destroy Judah for David’s sake and the promised lamp; Chronicles names David’s house, covenant and lamp for his sons. The shared promise is retained with the different objects Judah and David’s house.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Edom separates and appoints its own king
rationale: Both state that Edom breaks away from Judah and makes a king over itself in Joram’s days, matching the particular political separation rather than another revolt.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Joram strikes encircling Edom and the people flee
rationale: Both describe Joram going out, striking encircling Edom and chariot commanders, and the people fleeing. Kings names Sior and Chronicles adds by night; those details are not inserted into the other account.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel with preserved place forms: Edom’s continuing separation
rationale: Both state Edom remains separated from Judah and name an additional rebellion at that time. Kings has Lobena, Chronicles Lomna and an added abandonment-of-the-Lord explanation; the distinct forms and additional explanation remain visible.

relationship: Literary regnal formula: the remaining acts in Judah’s royal records
rationale: Joram’s closing formula refers his remaining acts to Judah’s royal daily records; Jehoshaphat’s closing formula similarly directs the reader to Judah’s royal annals. These are different kings’ notices, and the unavailable annals are not claimed as read.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel: Ahaziah succeeds his father Joram
rationale: Kings reports Joram’s death and burial followed by his son Ahaziah reigning; Chronicles likewise names Ahaziah son of Joram installed in his father’s place, adding the account of the older sons without equating any burial wording.

relationship: Repeated regnal identity with an unresolved synchronism difference
rationale: Both name Ahaziah becoming king in Judah during Joram of Israel’s reign; this notice gives the twelfth year, whereas the later notice gives the eleventh. The named succession is matched while the year difference remains unresolved.

relationship: Regnal narrative parallel with an unresolved accession-age difference
rationale: Both give Ahaziah one year reigning in Jerusalem and name his mother Athaliah daughter of Omri; Kings says he was twenty-two at accession, while Chronicles says twenty. The shared reign and maternal notice do not resolve that age difference.

relationship: Regnal assessment parallel: Ahaziah’s conduct follows Ahab’s house
rationale: Kings says Ahaziah walks in Ahab’s house’s way and does evil as that house did; Chronicles repeats that pattern while adding his mother’s and other counselors’ influence, retaining those added explanations in Chronicles.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: allied war against Hazael and Joram’s wounds
rationale: Both describe Ahaziah joining Joram son of Ahab against Hazael and Joram being struck; Kings names Remmoth-gilead and Syrians, while Chronicles has Rama-galaad and archers. The forms and different actor descriptions remain preserved.

relationship: Historical narrative parallel: Joram’s treatment and Ahaziah’s visit
rationale: Both place wounded Joram’s return for treatment at Jezreel or Jezrael and Ahaziah son of Joram’s visit because he is ill, retaining the distinct place forms and the two Joram parentages rather than merging the kings.
